claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has a fine-grained FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy initially has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
The as-built FCC microstructure is ductile and has no significant grain-boundary degradation.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by selective attack at grain boundaries by oxidizing or reducing species.
Selective grain-boundary attack causes local elemental segregation.
Oxidizing exposure produces brittle oxide phases at grain boundaries.
Reducing exposure may produce alternate non-oxide, nonductile phases at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation and brittle phase formation disrupt cohesive bonding and reduce intergranular strength.
Weakened grain boundaries promote crack initiation and rapid catastrophic failure under sustained stress.
Suppressing oxidation in a reducing atmosphere may alter diffusion-driven segregation.
Relative to the as-manufactured baseline, oxidizing exposure will increase intergranular oxide formation.
Relative to the baseline, oxidizing exposure will increase grain-boundary embrittlement.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce fracture toughness and ductility.
Reducing exposure will cause less grain-boundary degradation than oxidizing exposure.
Mechanical-property deterioration directly correlates with the degree of oxidation-induced segregation.
The proposed behavior becomes pronounced above approximately 700 °C.
Exposure for tens to hundreds of hours is sufficient for significant diffusion and oxidation.

contradictions.description: Reducing exposure is initially described as a possible source of preferential grain-boundary attack and alternate nonductile phases, but it is later described primarily as suppressing oxidation and producing less boundary degradation. The direction and role of the reducing-gas effect are therefore internally inconsistent.
